Gallery of recipes

Source: vignettes/gallery.Rmd
gallery.Rmd

Each recipe below is one complete example on real data, with a short note on what the verbs do and why the plot is built that way. Copy the code, swap in your own matrix, and adjust.

library(ggcalor)
# Optional: the fonts used on this page (any installed font works).
options(ggcalor.family = "Fira Sans", ggcalor.mono = "Roboto Mono")

Clustered heatmap with annotations

The dune data from vegan records the cover (on a 1–9 scale) of 30 plant species in 20 Dutch meadows, along with how each meadow is managed and how wet it is. A clustered heatmap shows which species occur together and which sites are alike.

data(dune, dune.env, package = "vegan")
sites <- data.frame(management = dune.env$Management, moisture = dune.env$Moisture,
                    row.names = rownames(dune))
levels(sites$management) <- c("biological", "hobby", "nature reserve", "standard")

ggcalor(t(dune), cell_size = 4.2) +
  calor_dendro(rows = TRUE, cols = TRUE) +
  calor_split(cols = 3) +
  calor_anno(top = sites) +
  calor_margin(right = "mean", fill = "#3B8F5C") +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlGn", direction = 1) +
  labs(title = "Wet meadows grow their own plant community",
       subtitle = "Cover of 30 plant species in 20 Dutch dune meadows",
       caption = "Data: vegan::dune", fill = "cover")

calor_dendro() clusters both axes and draws the trees. calor_split(cols = 3) cuts the column tree into three groups and separates them with a gap; cells stay square and each slice keeps its own subtree. The trees stay in ink here so that colour is left for the tracks; to colour the groups instead, see k and highlight in the recipe on scaled columns.

calor_anno() takes a data frame whose row names match the columns. Each column becomes one track. Unordered factors get distinct qualitative colours, and ordered factors such as moisture get a light-to-dark sequence. calor_margin(right = "mean") adds a bar of each species’ mean cover.

The final order is available for reuse, for example to order a table the same way:

p <- ggcalor(t(dune)) + calor_dendro(rows = TRUE, cols = TRUE)
str(calor_order_of(p))
#> List of 2
#>  $ rows: chr [1:30] "Poatriv" "Lolipere" "Poaprat" "Eleopalu" ...
#>  $ cols: chr [1:20] "11" "18" "17" "19" ...

Your own plots beside the heatmap

calor_panel() attaches any ggplot to a side of the heatmap. Map the row names to y (for a left or right panel) or the column names to x (for a top or bottom panel) and write the rest as ordinary ggplot2 code: geoms, scales, themes and labels are kept as you wrote them. ggcalor only lines the names up with the cells, after clustering, ordering and splitting.

m <- t(dune)
species <- data.frame(species = rownames(m), mean = rowMeans(m),
                      se = apply(m, 1, sd) / sqrt(ncol(m)))
bars <- ggplot(species, aes(mean, species)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3B8F5C", width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = mean - se, xmax = mean + se), width = 0.3, linewidth = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "mean cover \u00b1 se") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8)

present <- data.frame(site = rep(colnames(m), each = nrow(m)), cover = as.vector(m))
present <- present[present$cover > 0, ]
boxes <- ggplot(present, aes(site, cover)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.6, fill = "#D7EBDC", outlier.size = 0.4, linewidth = 0.3) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8)

ggcalor(m, cell_size = 4.2) +
  calor_dendro(rows = TRUE, cols = TRUE) +
  calor_split(cols = 3) +
  calor_panel(bars, side = "right", size = 28) +
  calor_panel(boxes, side = "top", size = 18) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlGn", direction = 1) +
  labs(fill = "cover")

The boxplots follow the clustered site order, gaps included, and the bars follow the species. Because the panels match by name, the order of rows in your data frame does not matter. A legend in a panel (say, bars filled by group) joins the heatmap’s legends.

Next to other plots

A ggcalor plot combines with any other ggplot through patchwork. The cells act as the heatmap’s panel, so neighbouring panels line up with the first and last row of cells, while the trees, tracks and legends take the space around them.

The heatmap has a fixed size, so give its column a width of NA in plot_layout(); patchwork 1.3 fails on a fixed-size plot with a numeric width.

library(patchwork)
pca <- prcomp(dune)
sites_pca <- data.frame(pca$x[, 1:2], moisture = dune.env$Moisture)
scatter <- ggplot(sites_pca, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = moisture)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Blues") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9, base_family = "Fira Sans")

heat <- ggcalor(t(dune), cell_size = 3.2) +
  calor_dendro(rows = TRUE, cols = TRUE, k = 3) +
  calor_anno(top = sites["moisture"]) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlGn", direction = 1) +
  labs(fill = "cover")

heat + scatter + plot_layout(widths = c(NA, 1)) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

Scaled columns, glyphs and brackets

When columns are measured in different units, scale them first. scale = "column" z-scores every column, so each cell shows how far a car sits from the average for that variable.

vars <- c("cyl", "disp", "hp", "carb", "wt", "drat", "gear", "mpg", "qsec")
group <- rep(c("engine", "chassis", "performance"), c(4, 3, 2))
transmission <- ifelse(mtcars$am == 1, "manual", "automatic")

ggcalor(as.matrix(mtcars[, vars]), cell_size = 4, scale = "column") +
  calor_dendro(rows = TRUE, k = 2, highlight = TRUE) +
  calor_split(rows = 2) +
  calor_anno(left = list(transmission = transmission), type = "glyph") +
  calor_bracket(cols = group, side = "bottom", angle = 90, size = 14) +
  calor_legend("histogram") +
  labs(title = "Light, frugal cars stand apart from the rest",
       subtitle = "Each specification as a z-score across 32 cars",
       caption = "Data: datasets::mtcars", fill = "z-score")

type = "glyph" draws a categorical track as symbols rather than coloured tiles. This keeps the colour for the heatmap itself. calor_bracket() labels runs of adjacent columns. calor_legend("histogram") replaces the colour bar with a histogram of all values painted in the fill scale, so the legend also shows how the values are distributed.

Oncoprint

A character matrix gets a discrete fill. luad_alterations has one row per gene and one column per TCGA lung adenocarcinoma, with NA where a gene is not altered. To keep the cells square at a readable width, we keep the ten most often altered genes and the tumours altered in at least one of them.

alt_colours <- c(mutation = "#3B8F5C", amplification = "#E4572E",
                 `deep deletion` = "#2E86AB", `mutation + amplification` = "#8E5BA8")

n_altered <- rowSums(!is.na(luad_alterations))
m <- luad_alterations[order(n_altered, decreasing = TRUE)[1:10], ]
m <- m[, colSums(!is.na(m)) > 0]

ggcalor(m, cell_size = 2.6, cell_gap = 0.25, border = NA, labels = "rows") +
  calor_order(rows = "sum", cols = "memo") +
  calor_margin(right = "sum", top = "sum", size = 10) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = alt_colours, breaks = names(alt_colours), na.value = "#F1EEE8") +
  labs(title = "KRAS and BRAF are rarely altered in the same tumour",
       subtitle = "RAS/RAF/MEK/JNK pathway alterations in 106 lung adenocarcinomas",
       caption = "Data: TCGA via cBioPortal", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

calor_order(rows = "sum") puts the most frequently altered genes on top. cols = "memo" is the memo sort used by cBioPortal. It orders samples so that those altered in the top gene come first, then the next gene, and so on, which turns mutual exclusivity into a staircase. Giving breaks in scale_fill_manual() keeps the empty cells (NA) painted with na.value but out of the legend. labels = "rows" shows the gene names and hides the sample IDs, which say nothing here.

Correlation matrix

Order first, then mask. Here the variables are ordered by clustering on 1 - r, and mask = upper.tri(cm) hides the redundant upper triangle. A transparent na_fill makes the masked cells disappear.

cm <- cor(mtcars)
o <- hclust(as.dist(1 - cm))$order
cm <- cm[o, o]

ggcalor(cm, cell_size = 8, mask = upper.tri(cm), cell_gap = 0.08, border = NA, na_fill = NA) +
  calor_text(digits = 2, size = 5.5) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdBu", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Heavier cars go fewer miles per gallon",
       subtitle = "Correlations between the specifications of 32 cars",
       caption = "Data: datasets::mtcars", fill = "r")

Setting limits = c(-1, 1) centres the diverging palette on zero and keeps the colour bar on the full range of a correlation.

Calendar heatmaps

A month-by-year grid is a heatmap too. AirPassengers gives monthly airline passengers (in thousands) from 1949 to 1960.

air <- matrix(AirPassengers, 12, dimnames = list(month.abb, 1949:1960))

ggcalor(air, cell_size = 7, cell_gap = 0.1, border = NA) +
  calor_text(digits = 0, size = 5) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1) +
  labs(title = "Air travel grew every year and peaked every summer",
       subtitle = "Monthly airline passengers, 1949–1960",
       caption = "Data: datasets::AirPassengers", fill = "passengers\n(thousands)")

Both the growth over the years (left to right) and the summer peak each year (July and August) show up at once. calor_radial() bends the same grid into a ring, with years running outwards from 1949 in the middle:

ggcalor(t(air)[12:1, ], cell_size = 4, cell_gap = 0.1, border = NA) +
  calor_radial(inner.radius = 0.3, gap = 0.35, legend = "right", label_size = 8) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1) +
  labs(fill = "passengers\n(thousands)")

Flat or round

global_temp holds NASA’s global temperature anomaly for every month from 1880 to 2025, as a 12-by-146 matrix of months by years. With this many columns, calor_labels(every = ) keeps every twentieth year and every third month. A diverging palette with symmetric limits puts the 1951–1980 average at white.

anomaly <- scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdBu", limits = c(-1.5, 1.5), breaks = c(-1, 0, 1),
                                labels = c("−1 °C", "0", "+1 °C"))

ggcalor(global_temp, cell_size = 2.2, border = NA) +
  calor_labels(every = c(rows = 3, cols = 20)) +
  anomaly +
  labs(title = "Every month of the last decade was warmer than any before 1980",
       subtitle = "Global temperature anomaly by month, against the 1951–1980 average",
       caption = "Data: NASA GISTEMP v4", fill = NULL)

Adding calor_radial() bends the same plot into a ring. The legend becomes a slim bar below the ring; legend = "right" or "inside" moves it.

ggcalor(global_temp, cell_size = 2.6, border = NA) +
  calor_radial(inner.radius = 0.4, gap = 0.25, label_size = 8) +
  calor_labels(every = c(rows = 3, cols = 20)) +
  anomaly +
  labs(title = "A planet running a fever",
       subtitle = "Global temperature anomaly by month, 1880–2025",
       caption = "Data: NASA GISTEMP v4", fill = "against the 1951–1980 average")

Smooth surfaces

When rows and columns are positions on a regular grid, like the heights of the Maunga Whau volcano in volcano, a smooth surface reads better than cells. smooth = "contour" interpolates the matrix onto a finer grid, blurs it by smooth_sigma cells, and draws filled contour bands at rounded break values.

v <- t(volcano[seq(87, 1, -2), seq(1, 61, 2)])
dimnames(v) <- list(seq_len(nrow(v)), seq_len(ncol(v)))

ggcalor(v, cell_size = 2.4, smooth = "contour", smooth_sigma = 1, labels = "none") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "mako") +
  labs(title = "Maunga Whau rises 100 m above its plain",
       caption = "Data: datasets::volcano", fill = "height (m)")

smooth = "raster" draws the same surface as a continuous image:

ggcalor(v, cell_size = 2.4, smooth = "raster", labels = "none") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako") +
  labs(fill = "height (m)")

Hex cells

cell_shape = "hex" tiles the grid with hexagons, offsetting every other row.

hx <- volcano[seq(1, 87, 5), seq(1, 61, 4)]
dimnames(hx) <- list(seq_len(nrow(hx)), seq_len(ncol(hx)))

ggcalor(hx, cell_shape = "hex", cell_size = 5, cell_gap = 0.06, labels = "none") +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Spectral") +
  labs(fill = "height (m)")

Waffle charts

calor_waffle() draws counts as a grid of unit cells, one waffle per group. Here each square is 1% of the penguins sampled on each island.

penguins <- as.data.frame(table(island = palmerpenguins::penguins$island,
                                species = palmerpenguins::penguins$species))
calor_waffle(penguins, "species", "Freq", by = "island", cell_size = 3.2) +
  labs(title = "Gentoo penguins live only on Biscoe",
       subtitle = "Share of each species among the penguins sampled on three islands")

Interactive

With ggiraph installed, calor_interactive() adds tooltips to the cells and categorical tracks, and hovering a cell highlights its whole row (or column, with data_id = "col"). calor_girafe() renders the result as an HTML widget.

p <- ggcalor(t(dune), cell_size = 4.2) +
  calor_dendro(rows = TRUE, cols = TRUE) +
  calor_anno(top = sites) +
  calor_interactive(data_id = "row")
calor_girafe(p)

Saving

A ggcalor plot knows its own size: the cells, trees, tracks, labels and legend add up to a fixed width and height in millimetres. calor_size() reports it, and calor_save() passes it to ggsave(), so the file holds exactly the plot you built with no squashed cells or empty borders.

calor_size(p)
calor_save(p, "dune.pdf")
calor_save(p, "dune.png", dpi = 300)
